findings.title: Storm-2372 conducts device code phishing campaign
findings.summary_md: Microsoft disclosed a campaign it tracks as Storm-2372, active since August 2024, that used Teams meeting invitations and messaging-app lures to get victims to enter attacker-generated device codes. The actor captured access and refresh tokens, then used Microsoft Graph to search mail and exfiltrate messages; Microsoft assessed with moderate confidence that the activity aligned with Russian interests. A February 14 update documented a switch to the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID, enabling device registration and issuance of a Primary Refresh Token. Microsoft recommended blocking device code flow in Conditional Access where it is not needed and revoking refresh tokens with revokeSignInSessions.

findings.title: Multiple Russian Threat Actors Targeting Microsoft Device Code Authentication
findings.summary_md: Volexity documented distinct Russian-linked clusters UTA0304, UTA0307 and activity it linked with medium confidence to CozyLarch using Device Code OAuth phishing against Microsoft 365 accounts. Lures included fake Element chat invitations and US Department of State or European Parliament meeting requests; UTA0307 hosted a page at connect-71q.pages[.]dev that generated fresh codes on demand to avoid the 15-minute expiry. Volexity observed FileDownloaded operations in M365 audit data and, in one case, an attacker-added application authorization. The report gave a detection method based on Entra sign-in logs where authenticationProtocol is deviceCode, and said blocking the device code flow in Conditional Access stopped the technique in its tests.

findings.title: OAuth Device Code Phishing Hits 340+ Microsoft 365 Organizations
findings.summary_md: The Cloud Security Alliance research note traces device code phishing from Storm-2372 activity through the EvilTokens PhaaS service, which it says launched on Telegram on February 16, 2026. It reports that a campaign first seen on February 19 reached 340 or more Microsoft 365 organizations in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Germany by mid-March. The note describes token polling from five Railway.com addresses, with three accounting for about 84 percent of events, and HTTP markers including /api/device/start paths and the X-Antibot-Token header. It recommends Conditional Access blocking of Device Code Flow, a 90-day Entra sign-in log review for authenticationProtocol: deviceCode, and explicit revokeSignInSessions calls because password resets do not kill refresh tokens.

findings.title: Inside an AI-enabled device code phishing campaign
findings.summary_md: Microsoft Defender Security Research described a widespread campaign that used Railway.com nodes and dynamic device code generation to defeat the standard 15-minute code lifetime. Lures were tailored by role with themes including RFPs, invoices and manufacturing workflows, and landing pages used Vercel, Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda redirects plus the X-Antibot-Token header on /api/device/start requests. After token capture the actors created malicious inbox rules, ran Microsoft Graph reconnaissance against finance and executive accounts, and in some cases registered devices within 10 minutes to obtain a Primary Refresh Token. Microsoft advised blocking Device Code Flow in Conditional Access, enabling Safe Links, revoking refresh tokens and temporarily disabling accounts during containment because access tokens can remain live for up to an hour.

findings.title: Device Code Phishing is an Evolution in Identity Takeover
findings.summary_md: Proofpoint describes device code phishing as a mass-market technique after criminal toolkits and PhaaS offerings appeared in fall 2025, with most activity aimed at Microsoft accounts and lower-volume Google-themed campaigns. It observed about seven near-identical variants in a 10-day window in April 2026 and says actor TA4903 shifted almost entirely to the technique, using PDF lures that sometimes had blank email bodies and QR codes. Dynamic code generation on link click removed the old 15-minute expiry constraint, and kits such as EvilTokens, Tycoon 2FA, ODx and Kali365 lowered the barrier to entry. Proofpoint notes that some April campaigns used PDFs that impersonated SharePoint documents and carried metadata artifacts from earlier Tycoon activity.

findings.title: Inside Wazza: A Newly Observed Device Code Phishing Kit Targeting Microsoft 365 Accounts
findings.summary_md: LevelBlue SpiderLabs tracked a multi-stage kit it calls Wazza, active since at least early July 2026 and still running in October. Emails originated from compromised accounts and carried business-themed PDF lures; the infrastructure used Google Sites, Cloudflare Workers, .com and .eu domains. The final pages impersonated Adobe, DocuSign and OneDrive and walked victims through Microsoft's device authorization flow. The report notes campaign parameters, decoy websites and subdomain-based routines that let one kit serve multiple themes.

findings.title: MadApe: The Code That Opens the Door
findings.summary_md: Group-IB identified a previously undocumented kit it calls MadApe, delivered through PDF attachments that impersonate SharePoint file-sharing notices and refer to payments, invoices and contracts. The pages present a dynamically supplied device code, copy it to the clipboard on click, and send the victim to the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin portal; backend status tracking uses paths such as /api/code/status/ followed by a numeric ID and /api/code/entered. Group-IB found 155 root domains, with phishing components on 97, and says 117 of the 154 domains registered in 2026 were registered between mid-June and late August, 133 through one registrar. Lures appeared in at least nine languages, the earliest operator panel was seen on August 19, and the infrastructure counts are not victim counts.

findings.title: New MadApe Phishing Kit Abuses Microsoft Device Code Sign-In to Steal Account Tokens
findings.summary_md: Expert Insights reported Group-IB's MadApe finding on October 29, describing PDF lures styled as SharePoint sharing notices for payments, invoices and contracts. The kit routes victims through a SharePoint-style portal or a human-verification challenge before showing a device code and redirecting to Microsoft's own sign-in page. The report says templates also impersonate OneDrive, Teams, Adobe Acrobat and DocuSign, with lures in at least nine languages including Hebrew messages targeting recipients in Israel. It highlights Group-IB's advice to inventory device code use in Entra sign-in logs, test Conditional Access restrictions in report-only mode, and revoke sessions and refresh tokens during containment.

findings.title: The Hidden Relay: Inside a Device Code Phishing Kit That Never Shows the Code
findings.summary_md: KnowBe4 ThreatLabs analyzed an August 2026 phishing URL that ran a device code grant without ever showing the code to the victim, using an NDA-themed email wrapped in Mandrill click tracking and Cloudflare Workers redirects. The relay page embedded pre-staged Microsoft sign-in state, including ctx, flowToken and canary fields, before the victim submitted an email address, then posted to login.microsoftonline.com. The kit exposed a nine-character userCode with a 900-second lifetime internally while using autoRelay and redirect mode, so the browser went straight to Microsoft's device approval page. KnowBe4 says a decoded ctx token matched byte for byte with the token on the genuine Microsoft page, indicating a pre-opened session rather than an adversary-in-the-middle proxy.
